utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Tanaskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Tanaskovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We broke off yesterday with my question and your answer that you went to visit Mr. Vasiljevic in an ambulance in Uzice. My next question would be: Do you know how long Vasiljevic stayed in the hospital in Uzice, or maybe you don't know?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he stayed more than 30 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, perhaps, drive him back home with an ambulance from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember when he went back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, and after how long, see Mr. Vasiljevic in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would see him about two months after that when he was walking around with some crutches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back to another point. Do you remember that the day you drove Mr. Vasiljevic to the hospital in Uzice, that it was a holiday?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a holiday known as the Trinity, because both I and my father are religious people and on that day, you take wheat, boiled wheat, to the church and some vegetables and then the priest blesses it and it's a tradition; this was the tradition passed down from my grandfather - my father was still alive - and this was meant to ensure the health of the livestock and the harvest, a good harvest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we have already heard, the Holy Trinity there consists of three days. Which of those three days did you go to church?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the Sunday, the first day of the Trinity. It's always a Sunday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you something else. Do you know any other person called Mitar?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Mitar Knezevic, also known as the Chetnik. That was his nickname during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe this Mitar Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's rather short, of the same height as Mitar Vasiljevic. He had a beard, and he had a faulty eye; he couldn't see on one eye.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say a "faulty eye," do you mean he had an eye missing?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he had an eye but, I can't explain it, he couldn't see it. It was sort of all white. It was damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Savic, my name is Dermot Groome and I represent the Office of the Prosecutor, and I will be asking you a few questions regarding your testimony. I think you told us yesterday that before you drove an ambulance, you were an ordinary driver; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before that, I worked on my own with a truck for ten years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you became an ambulance driver, did you receive any special medical training or is it simply that you drive patients to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would drive patients. First I started driving patients who went for dialysis treatment from Visegrad to Foca. For a year, I was an apprentice and then, after a year, I was taken off as permanent staff member in the health centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now when you go out on a call as an ambulance driver, do you administer any type of medical assistance at the scene or do you simply carry that person back to the hospital where they can be treated?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If everything could not be done in Visegrad, I would drive them on, and if it's a more serious case, then somebody from the medical staff would accompany the patient [as interpreted] as an escort with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm trying to get at is, if you respond to the scene of an accident you, yourself, don't attempt to give medical treatment to the person; you simply carry them back to the Visegrad Health Centre or to one of the other hospitals; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's say responding to a traffic accident, it is clear that the person has already deceased, they are dead. Is it also your job to bring that body to a funeral parlor or to morgue or does somebody else have that job?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would take the person from the spot because I can never be sure whether the person is dead or not, so I would drive them to the closest medical institution. I don't necessarily have to drive the person to the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anybody else in the town of Visegrad who has the responsibility of moving bodies that -- it's confirmed that they've died, wherever they are found; does anybody else have that responsibility in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, there's the funeral society. They would take care of the dead. The company's called communal. They have the necessary equipment and take care of the transport. They take them either to the cemetery or to their home, to the village, wherever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall this past August speaking with an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor, a person by the name of Yves Roy? Do you remember speaking with him?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Sarajevo with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he interviewed you regarding knowledge you might have regarding this case; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he asked you questions and you responded with however you could, whatever knowledge you had on certain matters; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the end of the interview, Mr. Roy gave you an opportunity to add anything else that you wanted to add; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think in response to that opportunity, you said, "No thank you, really, I am just happy that you are so nice and kind." Did you say that to Mr. Roy?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Roy, he tape recorded this conversation. There was a tape recorder on the table and it was tape recorded; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked me whether he should write it down or tape record it and I said it was up to him, and then he tape recorded it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were aware that he was tape recording it and you consented to that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the course of that interview, one of the things, I believe, you said was that you had seen Milan Lukic's wedding; was that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what day that was?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't know the exact date. I was also at the wedding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you at the church part of the wedding or the part of the wedding at the registrar's office in town?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't attend either of those ceremonies. I was invited in the afternoon, at 3.00, to the hotel. I didn't attend the actual ceremony which took place in church and in the cultural centre. I didn't attend those because there were guests invited to various parts of the ceremony and I was among those who was invited to the hotel in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there a party in celebration of his wedding in the afternoon at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is where I attended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us some idea how much before the wedding did you receive your invitation to attend Milan Lukic's wedding, one week, two weeks; how much time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you attended this wedding, I take it that you dressed in some nice clothes to go to the wedding; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody dresses up for a wedding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Vasiljevic there at the wedding?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there. He was at the wedding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would we be correct in assuming that he, too, was dressed in nice clothes to attend the wedding?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now also in your statement, you were asked some questions about the people from Kosovo Polje and you had -- you said in your statement that there was a time when you went to Kosovo Polje and warned those people about a possible attack by paramilitaries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kosovo Polje had vegetables which was planted in May, tomatoes and other vegetables, and every year, I would purchase from them tomatoes and peppers. And I went over there and told them to flee, to take a boat and cross the Drina and flee wherever. I know all the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that just one time that you went and gave them a warning or were there -- was it more than once that you gave a warning to the people of Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once I went on that occasion. I had a cup of coffee with them, a whole litre of coffee with them, and I begged them; I told them to flee. They complained there was some paramilitaries coming and I said flee, seek shelter. These were my old neighbours and friends and that is why I warned them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to Kosovo Polje, did you take your ambulance?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you give us an idea about what time of day, was it daytime, night-time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was daytime. It was mid-day, maybe 1.00 or 2.00 in the afternoon, broad daylight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you give us some idea of when you went to Kosovo Polje and gave them this warning?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been sometime around the 10th of May. That is when the planting season is, in May, in the fifth month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I want to clear up something. Did they tell you about the paramilitaries or you told them about the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that people they did not know at all came and one of them said, "I hid ten litres of petrol in the field, and he found the petrol," but he said he'd never seen those people before. And I said, "I don't know them either. I'm afraid of them, too. We're all afraid. It's better for you to seek shelter, to get away."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, I want to read you a portion of the statement from this August and see, does it change your answer on this point. "I know that in 1992, in June, end of May or beginning of June, I went to Kosovo Polje, pretending to get some vegetables because it is a known area for growing vegetables and so when I go there and told them to move away from the area because of these paramilitary guys who will be coming. Many of them are thankful to me because they ran away that day across the river." And then Mr. Roy said, "So you've been nice to the Muslim population during the war and up to today?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down, please, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said, "They trusted me. And I told them they should move away from that area because these guys are coming. They are going to probably loot and who knows what you can expect from them so ..." So I want to ask you the question again, Mr. Savic: Wasn't it you who told the people in Kosovo Polje that there were paramilitaries planning to come to Kosovo Polje and possibly commit crimes against those people? Wasn't it you that told them?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to those people because one never knows. I didn't know where those people would go, but it was safer for them to go away. One never knew where they would crop up. Knowing these people, they all knew me. I would carry material to their homes regularly and buy vegetables from them, Bakima's mother. I knew each and every one of them by name. I said -- I begged them to move away. They were grateful. We had coffee. I sat with them. They asked me to stay longer, but I, too, was afraid to stay longer, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The precise question that I'm asking you, Mr. Savic, is: Wasn't it you who told them about paramilitaries rather than them telling you about the paramilitaries? It was you that pretended to go and get vegetables and to warn them about paramilitaries; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they had told me earlier on that they had already been visited by them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would I be correct in thinking that you had other friends in the Visegrad area that were also Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had a colleague that I gave cigarettes to. I bought 20 boxes and gave them to him and told him to go away. His name is Mujo Racic. I gave him these cigarettes and told him to seek shelter and he went across the hills. His wife took the cow. I even wanted to drive him to Priboj by car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aside from the people in Kosovo Polje, did you at any other time in May or June travel to another Muslim settlement and again warn those people that paramilitaries might be coming? Did you ever do that in any other settlement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. In the street behind the cultural centre of Hamid Besirevic, I took care of two children in my own home and then I took their mother, too. I dressed her in black clothes, my wife's clothes. I put them in my car, my vehicles, and took them to Priboj. Naila and her two children. They are now in Denmark and we are in touch. She worked as a cashier.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A doctor lady, I'm sorry, the interpreter corrects herself.

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, a lady doctor from Sase. Osman and Jasmina and their mother, I drove them to my sister's place in Uzice in June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, I don't mean to suggest that you were anything other than kind to Muslim people. What I do want to know, however, is did you warn any other people? Did you go to any other settlement, pretending to be there on other business, to warn people, or was Kosovo Polje the only time that you did this type of thing, this -- give this type of warning?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I came across a person in the street or in any settlement, I told them, "Please flee." It wasn't safe for anyone. No one could prove that he was a Serb or a Muslim or something. When unknown people under arms were walking around, you couldn't tell them what you were. I didn't have occasion to tell them who I was. So whenever I came across anyone I knew, I would tell them, "Flee, go and seek shelter wherever you can."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you then how was it that you knew that paramilitaries were planning to attack the village or the settlement of Kosovo Polje? What did you see or hear that made you believe that the people in Kosovo Polje were going to be attacked by paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fear that was widespread among all people and then people were roaming around like cattle. They were ready to kill, to steal. You don't know who that person is, what he is. He doesn't talk to anyone. He behaves like an animal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you estimate for us the first time you saw people walking around and behaving in this manner in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Yugoslav army had left Visegrad - they left on the 18th of May - after that, they arrived, some strange people that had their own laws. No one dared go out in the street, whether we were Serbs or Muslims. It was an impossible situation of fear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some people may have had the choice not to go out into the streets. My question to you is: Because of your job as an ambulance driver, did you have to go out and travel in the streets when these people were roaming around the streets?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to. There were people who were ill. There were heart patients. I had to go and pick them up and drive them to the centre. I was the only one who had to move around willy-nilly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during this time period, would it be fair to say that you, yourself, saw some of these men commit crimes, crimes such as looting or destroying property?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would see them, but I don't know these people. I didn't know them at all. They could do whatever they wanted. They could go wherever they wanted. They would break into apartments; they would do whatever they wanted. They were armed and they could do what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, yourself, see them engage in this activity?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, in the course of your duties, ever have to respond to a person who was the victim of a crime by some of these people, perhaps beaten up, perhaps shot? Did you ever have to carry one of those people to the Visegrad Health Centre?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, from Osanice. A woman came who had a bullet wound in her nose. She was treated and discharged. Then I drove some people to Priboj. The doctor would tell me, "Drive them there." It was at my own risk. I'd turn on the engine and drive them to Priboj. From Zepa, I took two or three children from a boat. They came in a boat. They had a white flag with a red cross on it, and I picked them up from the boat at the Drina and took them from Uzice. A man from Zepa called Osman had brought them in a boat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those children were injured?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were. That is why I drove them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your duties, did you ever have occasion to remove deceased, dead bodies, that it was clear to you people had been -- had died as a result of violence?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not me. Other people did that. But I never did that. I couldn't. It was not my duty anyway. It was not my responsibility to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your duties driving around the street, did you see dead bodies lying in the streets of Visegrad around this time period?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the streets. There weren't people in the streets. There would be some near the river, on the bank of the Drina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you approximate for us about how many bodies did you see lying on the bank of the Drina?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would see a couple of bodies, sometimes five, sometimes two, sometimes three, depended, ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you give us an idea of when the first time you saw bodies on the bank of the Drina was?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the beginning of June, May, end of May, beginning of June, maybe July even.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you approximate in total how many bodies did you see on the bank of the Drina, less than 100, more than 100?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say, but perhaps 100 even.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair for me to, or would I be correct in thinking that of the injured people that you had contact with and the -- any of these dead bodies that you were able to recognise, that predominantly they were Muslims from Visegrad? Would I be correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the bodies along the bank of the river, would people passing by on the streets of Visegrad, let's say in the square, over the bridge, would they have been able to see these bodies as well?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depended. Sometimes the river -- waters of the Drina would rise several metres and then they would go downstream. The water would take them downstream when the river was high, so that's what would happen mostly. But people were afraid, they didn't like to look. Perhaps somebody would look but mostly people were afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the point is, if somebody did want to look, they were easily visible to people walking across the bridge or on the streets of Visegrad; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If somebody wanted to see on purpose, they could see. Anybody could see, whoever wanted to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that when the river would rise, the bodies would be washed downstream. The water level of the Drina in this particular point is controlled by the dam. It's not a function of rain, but it's a function of how much water is released from the dam; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would I be correct in thinking that from time to time, somebody went to the dam, released an amount of water that then flushed these bodies down, away from the town? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there were people working on the dam, who worked there. They were on duty there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would I also be correct in thinking that in the course of your duties, you had to cross the old Drina bridge many times a day?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes I had to, depending on the requirements. Sometimes I would have to cross five times, sometimes not at all and sometimes even ten times. It all depended. But we tried to save on fuel, so if there wasn't any great necessity, I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you crossed the old Drina bridge, did you ever see any indications of violence on the bridge, perhaps blood stains, perhaps broken teeth or articles of clothing? Did you see anything that indicated to you that there were violent acts being committed on the bridge itself?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was blood, but I didn't see any clothing or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would the blood that you saw, was it concentrated in the area of what's called the sofa and it's the stone seat that is on the bridge? Is that where you saw the blood?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just on the sofa, around there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see blood on the sofa of the bridge throughout this period from May throughout the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from May to July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, ever see any crimes being committed on the sofa of that bridge?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that. They did that mostly at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, without -- you don't have to tell us the exact address of your house, but can you give us an idea of where your apartment or where your home is with respect to the bridge?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's 1.300 metres in the direction of the bridge, upstream. I can't see the bridge from my house. You can't see the bridge from my house. If you were to go up on to the roof, you would be able to see it, so it's about 1.500 metres. My house is not turned towards the bridge. It doesn't face the bridge. It's in a more densely-populated area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, during this period of time during your travels as an ambulance driver, did you see homes that you knew belonged to Muslim people that appeared to you to have been looted and then burned?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were belonging to individuals, there were some burnt houses, but not in my street, not a single one was burnt in my street. When the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. war began, two Serbs houses were burned town, Pecikoza and Mica Savic, a neighbour of mine, and then later on, Murat Sabanovic's house, in the part where I passed by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you approximate for us the number of houses that you knew to be Muslim that you saw burning or burnt down during this time period in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around me, no houses were on fire. Opposite me, the first house next door was burnt down. I wasn't at home at the time. It's a house that's 15 metres away from me, so my next door neighbour's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aside from your immediate neighbourhood, in the areas of Visegrad that you travelled, can you approximate for us how many houses you saw burnt down belonging to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, I saw some, but I didn't know. You would see some smoke rising from somewhere, but -- well, five or six houses, maybe ten. Opposite me, the street called Pionirska, I think maybe one or two over there. I saw that they had burnt down later on. I don't know when they were actually burning, but I saw the effects later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the school up on Pionirska Street, the Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Two of my sons went to that school. I went to parent/teacher evenings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us where your neighbourhood is or where your house is with respect to that school? How far away from that school is your house?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the crow flies, about 600 to 700 metres, and the way children go, the route children take, a little longer because you have to go through town. You couldn't cut across the settlement. So as the crow flies, it would be 500, 600 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a small creek that runs parallel to Pionirska Street, or perhaps a sewage ditch?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A creek, I have my part of the creek there, too. My property borders on the creek, the upper part towards the end of the creek. I have my -- what I inherited from my father, the piece of land that belongs to me now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if somebody were to walk directly across from the school and reach that creek, if they walked along that creek, they would reach your property, your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the left, 100 metres from the creek. Towards the end of the creek, then 100 metres away is my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say you saw two houses burning on Pionirska Street. Can you give us an idea of when you saw those houses burning?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up above, one was burning on the 1st of May. It belonged to a neighbour, Ibrahim was his name, Hodza, and his house was alight on the 1st of May, not the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the other house that you described as having seen burn, when was that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say when the other one was burning. They are lower down from me and I wasn't at home even my neighbour's house was burning. My neighbours tried to put it out. Now, I know that somebody had set the Hodza's house on fire. As to the other one down -- further down, I don't know. I know where they are, but I don't know when they were burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The neighbour that was a Hodza, did he have a horse or own a horse?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He had a house in the countryside and he had a house there and he would come from time to time, and I know that people from Serbia, from Yugoslavia, would come by and he would read them things. It's across the road from my house. Ten or fifteen people would come from Serbia and he would look through some books for them, read something out of some books. And he had a house in the countryside, in Dobovik, near the village of Dobovik. His wife and my mother are next door neighbours there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far away is this village where he had the country house from where he lived?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight or nine kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how would you -- if I were standing at the school, at Karadzic school, how -- what would be the quickest way for me to get to his country house? Would it be to continue walking up Pionirska Street or to go back down into the town?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would continue up the hill. You wouldn't go back towards town. Selo, Babin Potok and then Dobovic, that's how you'd go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the second house that you saw burning on Pionirska Street, could you give us an idea where that house is with respect to the school? Could you help orient us as to where that house was?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the school, 50 metres, 100 metres in front of the school to the left, on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that house close to the creek?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Close to the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was close to the street?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nearer the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the person that owned that house?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a policeman, Memic Mujo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you learn about his house being burnt?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I would go towards my own house, the street -- my street is up above, his house is down below, and it's 50 metres away and you could see it, and I knew where everybody's house was all over Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you actually see that house the night that it was set afire?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't see it then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you first learnt of that house being burnt when you looked down from your property and saw the house and saw that it was burnt? Is that how you learnt about that house being burnt?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a few questions about Mr. Vasiljevic. In addition to giving a statement to Investigator Roy, you also gave a statement to Mr. Tanaskovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was in May of the year 2000; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 4th of May, 2000, is when I gave the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you remember when you gave that statement to Mr. Tanaskovic that you told him that Mr. Vasiljevic had proclaimed himself to be the chief of hygiene in Visegrad. Do you remember telling that to Mr. Tanaskovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not chief of hygiene. I had my own chiefs of sanitary or hygiene department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read you a portion of that statement and see whether or not it refreshes your recollection: "During the war, I saw Vasiljevic in civilian clothes, with an arm band. He introduced himself as a chief of hygiene in the town of Visegrad." Do you remember telling Mr. Tanaskovic that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you told that to Mr. Tanaskovic, was that based upon you hearing Mr. Vasiljevic say, "I am the chief of hygiene," or was it based on something that somebody told you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear Mitar say that, but I heard that he had been assigned, I don't know how, but he was for cleaning the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that there's a difference between somebody who is assigned to cleaning the town and somebody who is the chief of hygiene for the town. There's a difference between those two positions, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there wasn't anybody there. Had Mitar not cleaned it, nobody would have cleaned it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what I'm interested in is this title of chief of hygiene. How did you come to learn or believe that he was the chief of hygiene?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what people would say, "Mitar is for the cleaning of the town." And some individuals gave him that kind of title. People were saying that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you spoke with Investigator Roy, you said something a bit different. Do you remember saying to Investigator Roy that Mr. Vasiljevic had proclaimed himself as mayor of the town? Do you remember saying that to Mr. Roy?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, I might have said that, for hygiene, for the cleanliness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you told Mr. Roy that Mitar Vasiljevic had proclaimed himself mayor of the town, what you really meant was that he was in charge of hygiene; is that what you're saying today?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the course of your travels around Visegrad during this period, did you see Mr. Vasiljevic clean the town?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And he would make the women and the men and everybody to clean in front of their own store or house where they were, that they should clean up in front of their own door because there were different party posters stuck over walls and everywhere. There was graffiti, so in one night you would have 100 new slogans written up, and he would tell people to clean up. He told my wife to clean up. He told Ranko Knezevic's wife and Bogdan Stanicic to clean up. He made him clean up, too. When he was passing by, he said, "Sir, you have to clean up what is in front of your place." So everybody did clean up. Nobody minded. They would clean everything up nicely. It wasn't a threat of any kind or anything like that, he would just tell them to clean up in front of their own door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how many times did you see him engage in this cleaning activity?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whenever I would pass by in the car, almost daily, every day when I would drive past. I didn't have much contact with anybody because I didn't have time so my movements were restricted and I would have -- I would pass by, but I would see him there in the centre whenever I passed by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you give us an idea over what period of time did this clean up occur, for one week, two weeks, a month? What was the period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it lasted from as soon as the Yugoslav army left, and then he saw to it regularly. He cleaned it regularly until he was injured and had to go to hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, can you help us? You've testified about how you took him to hospital. Can you help us, orient us regarding the time. This fire at Mr. Memic's house, did that occur before or after you took Mr. Vasiljevic to Uzice hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was after I had taken him, after that. Mitar went to hospital first, and then that was afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you approximate the time between the fire that you saw at the Memic house and your taking Mr. Vasiljevic to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I took him, I came back at around 23 hours and the next day, whether it was the next day or the day after, I saw that the house had been on fire. I wasn't there when it was -- when it was set fire to, but you know when you set fire to a house, the house smokes for the next three days. There's smoke coming out of it. It was summertime. Nobody bothered to put out the fire. It could even smoke for seven days. It has sort of this -- it sort of goes on, it's a process, and I think it was after that. I think that Mitar was transported first, transferred first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw the house, was it smoking?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you some houses smoke for three days afterwards. Nobody put the fires out. Well, the neighbours do so that the fire wouldn't expand to them, catch theirs, but the -- the furniture inside and the clothing or whatever is in the house can go on smoking for days, three days or more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what I'm asking you is this particular house, did you see this particular house smoking when you first saw it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I saw that the roof had burnt down, that there wasn't a roof on the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that the house that you saw burning was set on fire perhaps one, two, or even three days before the time you saw it? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many days before you saw it do you believe that the house was set on fire?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I saw it, it was -- it could have still been -- it might have been a day before. I didn't come home regularly. I spent the night in the hospital. I took Mitar there, and I had somewhere to sleep and have meals there, so I stayed there. And then when they would let me have a day off, I would go back home and then come back. So but for 30 days, sometimes, I didn't go home. I could sleep there, wash there. I had all the facilities over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The night that you took Mr. Vasiljevic to the hospital, did you sleep at the hospital that night?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if you slept at the hospital the night before?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I couldn't leave the health centre. You never knew when you would have a case, because there were only two drivers, so one would go off somewhere and the other one would be there if the need arose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you drove Mr. Vasiljevic to the hospital, when is the next day that you were able to go home?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you exactly. I can't remember. I would go when the doctors said I could go or I would ask, because it's only two kilometres by car. Was it the next day or perhaps -- I don't know, to visit my children. My children were small, they were 10 years old -- one was 6, one was 8, actually. So I would rush back home to see if they would need anything and that kind of thing. Sometimes I would go twice a day, sometimes once, sometimes not at all. I could rush back. So I can't actually say when I went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know how many days went between bringing Mr. Vasiljevic to the hospital and your next trip home; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Because I had to drive some patients the next day. Sometimes you would go three times during a day and night to Uzice and back, I would keep going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Back to the cleaning for a moment. Do you remember telling Mr. Roy that it was your impression that the people that were cleaning for Mr. Vasiljevic, that they were scared of him? Do you remember telling Mr. Roy that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember saying that, but they respected him. They had to do the work when -- well, not that they had to, he didn't force them in any bad sense, but it was good for all our health and for hygiene, so it was a sort of citizen's duty to listen to him and to clean up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me read you a portion of that tape-recorded statement and see if it does refresh your memory. "Really, people were scared of him and they would do that, and the town was never cleaner." Does that refresh your memory as to whether you told Mr. Roy that you believe that these people were scared of Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would have a drink too many sometimes so he might have been a bit bossy, "You have to do that and then you can go home." So everyone considered this to have been an order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you'll agree with me that that's somewhat different from people being afraid of him, correct? Being bossed by somebody and being afraid of them are two different things, wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he had no weapon to threaten with or anything. But he tried to make people see that it was their duty, but people were afraid of everything, you could say. We were all scared. I don't know how I could explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what I'm interested in is what do you yourself observe when you would see Mr. Vasiljevic and his cleaning crew? What did you, yourself, observe that made you believe that these people were frightened or scared of Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mostly women, including my own and others, one's house one lives in and works in and it provides you with a living, and he would say to her, "You have to clean it up." Then when he came back, he would see that it was clean, and they had to do what they were told. And that was the kind of fear I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that when he drinks, he would get a bit bossy. Would it be possible that some of these people who were working for him perceived his conduct when he was drinking as a bit aggressive? Would that have been possible?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would be a little more noisy, but he would never fight, or he would be a bit lighthearted. He would speak more loudly. We men knew his nature. He would sort of behave bossily but he wasn't dangerous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you a bit more about your duties as an ambulance driver. Can you give us an idea of, on average, how many calls would you go out on a day during this time period?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the day. Sometimes two, three, five, ten because, after all, most of the people had moved out. There weren't that many inhabitants. The number of the population had gone down, so up to ten, sometimes two, sometimes five, sometimes three. It depended on the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during this time period, I think you've told us that it was possible for you to work every day, that you may not have had a day off during the week; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes after 20 days or a month. I was under work obligation, and I wasn't allowed to move anywhere else. I had to be on duty, attached to the medical centre nonstop. It could go on for three months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during this time period, can you give us an idea of these patients between two and ten per day, how many of them would you say were Muslim patients, or were they predominantly Serb patients that you would carry to the health centre during May, June and July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the patients, they didn't come to see me, they went to see the doctor, and the more serious cases, by instructions from the doctor, I would have to drive them somewhere else. Sometimes I would have two, one or two to drive somewhere. Sometimes none. A lot of people came for medication to see the doctor. There would be up to 50 people waiting, depending how they felt. Most people were complaining of breathing problems, heart problems. They would come on foot and using whatever means they had to the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying that most of those patients were Serb, they were not Muslims, during May, June and July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In May, there were Muslims, but in June, Muslims no longer came, in June and July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would I also be correct in saying that of the people you carried to the hospital during that period of time, by and large, most of them were Serb as well?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June and July, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we've heard a great deal of evidence during this trial that could lead us to believe that during the June and July of 1992, a large number of Muslims were injured. Were you ever called to respond and carry an injured Muslim to the hospital in Visegrad? I'm sorry, could you repeat your answer a little louder? I don't think it was picked up by the microphone?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not ever, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we know of at least two quite notorious fires in Visegrad where people were injured and died. Were you ever called, perhaps as part of a fire brigade, to respond to locations of two fires and to help transport injured people to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not. I know that my colleague, I think he was killed, this colleague of mine. He drove a little girl to Titovo Uzice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mr. Savic: It seems from your testimony that you've always been kind to Muslims. Would it have been safe for you during this period to go out and to help an injured Muslim, perhaps one that was injured by these paramilitaries you told us about? Would it have been safe for you to go out and to transport that person to either Visegrad hospital or Foca hospital or Uzice hospital? Would that have been safe for you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I was driving alone to Uzice, it wouldn't be safe. I would have to hide someone. If the doctor gives me instructions, but even he didn't feel safe, so I did it on my own risk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not as concerned as to where you might bring them as the simple fact of was it safe for you to give assistance to injured Muslims, Muslims injured by paramilitary activity or some other physical violence during this time period? Was it safe for you to respond and carry them?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, why was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't dare because I was as afraid as they were. Paramilitaries would attack anyone. How can I prove who I am and who is he and why are you doing this or that? And then I would be exposing myself to danger, so it wasn't the same to me what would happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, am I correct in thinking that your ambulance is somehow marked as an ambulance, it has a red cross and lights to indicate that it is an ambulance?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And am I correct in thinking that you are now telling us that even in a marked ambulance, you did not feel it was safe to go and render assistance to Muslims injured by violence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never safe. There would be a rotating light; there was a red cross. People got killed here near Rude, a doctor, a driver and a nurse, they all got killed. They would shoot at them, too. It depends what area you got into. Nobody paid attention to anything anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, it seems that I can conclude from what you are telling us that you were able to go out and render assistance to between two and ten Serb people during this period, but that it was not safe for you to go out and render assistance to any Muslims during this period. Is my conclusion correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. In the street and in town, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my question to you now is: Why was it not safe for you to give assistance to an injured Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people coming from the outside, people I didn't know, and you couldn't negotiate with them. You couldn't say to them, "Look, here, friend" - I don't even know how to address him - sir, gentlemen, there's no explanation. He won't let you talk, he's just not interested. They didn't care about us either. As the local people of Visegrad, they didn't care. They didn't know people by name. I would have to take out my ID to show them who I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, were you ever given an instruction through the health centre or perhaps through some of the politicians or government people in town, was an instruction ever conveyed to you that Muslim people should not be assisted if they were injured during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Never. No one ever said that we shouldn't assist. In fact, the doctors felt we should assist everyone, and whoever came to the health centre, the doctors would treat them and assist them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know a person by the name of Behija Zukic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. She worked with my brother in France for six years. They were good friends and we were on very good terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you familiar with the shop that she owned?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. She gave me vegetables sometimes. When my brother came from Belgrade who used to be with her in France, she would give me some vegetables to take to my mother because he helped her with the documents in France. When she came to France, he helped her with the administration and with the authorities, and we were on very good terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you familiar with a red Volkswagen Passat car that she Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. owned?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do know, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's been testimony in this case regarding a day at which her body was brought to the Visegrad health centre. Do you recall if you were working the day that Mrs. Zukic's body was brought to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think it was brought there at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when she died?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when, but I heard that she had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you hear had killed her?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably whoever was driving the Passat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you see driving the Passat after her death?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you see him driving that Passat?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For two months, he drove it nonstop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that during that two-month period, you saw that car just about every day?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In passing. In passing, yes, I would see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, is it important to know which Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the first name of the Lukic who you are referring to now? Was it Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to answer verbally so the --

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever see --

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Milan Lukic. Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever see Sredoje Lukic driving in that car as well?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mitar Vasiljevic driving in that car?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mitar never drove a car, nor did he ever drive in that car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me correct -- I mean, did you ever see Sredoje Lukic as a passenger in that car?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. He may have been, but I didn't see him. He drove another car, Sredoje did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic has told us about at least one occasion on which he was in that car. Did you ever see Mr. Vasiljevic driving or as a passenger in that car?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I didn't see him. I didn't see Mitar in that car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying that the Muslim population of Visegrad was very fearful about that car?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The witness is indicating he's not hearing anything through his headset.

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were indeed afraid. People fled from it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us why people were afraid of that car?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard he would pick up people at night in that car and take them off somewhere, where, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it your understanding that these people would then possibly be killed?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Possibly be raped?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I had my own suspicions that those people might be killed. Everyone was afraid. I didn't see women, but I did see people -- men being afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that some of the people that were taken away in that car were tortured?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've just told us about your own suspicion regarding what happened when people were taken in that car. You seem like a very reasonable person. Can you tell us upon what you base that suspicion? Can you think of -- what did you actually see or hear that made you suspicious of what would happen to people in that car?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't care much about those people. That's why he picked them up, I suppose. He picked them up to eliminate them. Surely, he didn't take them out for lunch. I never saw anything like that in my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The times that you saw him pick up these people, was Milan Lukic armed with a weapon?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He always had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when was it that you first became aware that this red Passat and Milan Lukic were involved in this kind of conduct that you're describing, taking people away and liquidating them? When did you first become aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost immediately after the Yugoslav army left. Maybe it was the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you say that it became general knowledge in the town of Visegrad that this red Passat was being used to take away people and liquidate them?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes. As soon as I saw him driving it -- what he did, I don't know, I didn't like to look. I didn't have occasion to look and watch. But it's been proven now that that is what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be correct in thinking that by the beginning of June, most of the Serbs in the town of Visegrad were aware that this red Passat was being used in this manner?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, the Serbs, too, feared him because he did these things mostly at night, sometimes in the daytime, too, and every reasonable man avoided it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it true that during this period of time after the JNA left, that people would discuss this, perhaps at work, perhaps in coffee, cafes, after work, that people would discuss what Milan Lukic was doing in the town of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. It depended on what people said. Everyone was responsible for himself and it was difficult for anyone to understand that this was possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Your suspicions of what happened with this car, did you discuss that with any of your colleagues at work?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we couldn't. I don't know how to explain it to you. People found it strange. People couldn't dream that any such thing was possible. One didn't know what was going on. We didn't dare. These people didn't care who was who or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Would you have been surprised if, after the beginning of June, you met somebody who lived in Visegrad and worked in Visegrad and they didn't seem to know about what Milan Lukic was doing with this car? Would that strike you as odd?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are people that don't know, quite a lot of them were there and I wouldn't be surprised if half of them didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to the day that you responded to a call for help in the square in front of the Visegrad Hotel. My question to you is: When you arrived in front of the hotel and you saw Mr. Vasiljevic, was it clear to you from the very beginning that Mr. Vasiljevic had fallen off of a horse?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's quite certain. I claim that. I think the horse was standing somewhere, but I just sort of registered that the horse was somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any details of the horse?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know any details, how, when, where. I just know that it was there. That's all I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And correct me if I am wrong, but your recollection is that Mr. Vasiljevic had on civilian clothes on that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that -- so from the very first moment you arrive, it's clear to you that Mr. Vasiljevic, dressed in civilian clothes, is injured when he falls off a horse in the middle of the town; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what people told me, and we joked a little about it because this was a mayor and this was Mitar, you know, and we made fun of the whole thing a little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you are there and assisting Mr. Vasiljevic, no one ever comes up to you and says, "Mr. Savic, Mr. Vasiljevic was injured on a battle field." Nobody ever said anything to you of that nature; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, I believe you described the shirt that he was wearing as a dark shirt; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People wore different clothes that I drove around, so I -- there are different clothes, but I gave this matter some thought today and I think it was dark clothes. His uncle's son had got killed, and I think he wore dark clothes -- because really, it's hard to remember. I don't know what I was wearing the day before yesterday. I know what I wore yesterday but not the day before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you or recall for you a portion of the statement that you made to Investigator Roy and see if that changes the answer that you are giving us now. "If I can remember correctly, it was some very colourful T-shirt and some normal trousers." Do you remember telling Investigator Roy that on that day, Mr. Vasiljevic was wearing a very colourful T-shirt?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have said that because I know in civilian clothes, he had a T-shirt and a short windbreaker like this one, the one I am wearing. He never wore anything long. He always wore a short jacket, a leather jacket or something like this. But at the time, it was summer but it was overcast and raining.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just so that the transcript records what you are wearing, I will describe it and maybe just tell me if I've described it correctly. You are wearing a -- what appears to be a light jacket which comes down to about your waist. It has long sleeves and it has a collar on. Would that be a correct description of what you're wearing now?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is sports clothes, casual clothing, you know, the same length as this. And at the time, he -- as a waiter, he used to wear a normal suit jacket and a suit and a white shirt when he was on duty, but when he was not working, he would wear casual clothes like this, but short, a short jacket like mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just so we document what your jacket looks like, the description that I just gave regarding it, would you agree that that's a correct description of your jacket?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We call these jackets sports jackets, like this. Short ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, it may be a foreign expression, but I would call it a wind cheater.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm just trying to document the length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, the witness agrees with that.

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Windjammer, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me at least that it comes down to your waist? Can we agree with that much before the break?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it has long sleeves?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll resume again at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, just one or two more questions about what you recall about Mr. Vasiljevic's dress that day. Do you remember him wearing an arm band at this point in time when you first arrive and he's fallen off the horse?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A red band. It was just a plain band, nothing on it, I don't know what arm. I think it was the right that he had this band or ribbon around here like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've just indicated your right arm and above your elbow, in the area of your bicep; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, above the elbow, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall what colour that was?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Red.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did he appear to you, when you arrived, did he appear to you to be drunk?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was, a little. He wasn't actually "drunk drunk" like when you're really drunk, but he was tipsy, judging by the way he was talking and making a noise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say judging by the way he was talking, were his words somewhat slurred; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were clear, but loud.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you spoke to him, was he able to describe for you how he was injured and where he was injured?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found him there. I don't usually ask people, I just ask people to help me and to transport the patient as soon as possible. Possibly, he was saying something but I don't remember. I know that he called me "Zile," "What's up, Zile?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than that, do you recall having any other conversation with him before you put him into the ambulance?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Mostly they're behind my back. There is a partition between me, the driver, and the people behind, so whether he was talking or what he was saying to the people that helped us, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the people that helped you put him into the ambulance, can you tell us the names of the people you recall helping you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember now, but I know that Pero was there, Mitrovic, Pero Mitrovic, and the others who were with him, I don't know whether somebody else I know was there, I can't remember because, you know, lots of things have passed through my head since that time, lots of people, lots of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Ratko Simsic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a teacher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether or not you saw him there at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't there beside me. He wasn't there at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the drive from where you found Mr. Vasiljevic to the hospital is a relatively short drive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two, three minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's essentially just across the old Drina bridge?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Across the bridge and then another 300 or 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at the hospital, I would imagine that some of the nurses or some of the doctors would have asked you what kind of case you had and you would have responded you have somebody that fell off a horse. Would I be correct in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember specifically who it was that you told what the condition of Mr. Vasiljevic was and how he got into that condition?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told the nurse who was there, I don't know who it was, I know that Goran Loncarevic, the doctor came down and while he was on the spot, on the stretcher, he looked at him and concluded that the leg was broken and then sent him further on. There were two or three young men who took up the stretcher and took Mitar off to the, I think, X-ray department, but I didn't actually go upstairs to see, but you have to carry them up the steps 50 metres or so where the X-ray department is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell the nurse that you've referred to that you had somebody who had fallen off a horse? Did you tell that nurse that fact?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We told her that, and the doctor that, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's Dr. Loncarevic. You told Dr. Loncarevic that you had somebody who fell off a horse; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now during this time period when you are transporting people, is it true that you just transport civilians? You aren't working for the Territorial Defence transporting injured soldiers, were you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did transport wounded soldiers that came in from the field up to the health centre and they would give them to us. We had two old cars, a bigger van, which could accommodate an intravenous drip and so on and, if necessary, a nurse and a doctor could accompany the wounded person, and we used the kombi van where we would set up this drip and soldiers would go to Uzice in that, regardless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But am I correct in saying that as far as transporting soldiers injured on a battle field to town, there was a special unit that did that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a special unit and a driver on the battle field, but I would be assigned to the field, too, and if it was closer, if it was quicker for me to get to the wounded person from town, then I would do that, too. I would see that first aid was administered and then take them further on to hospital. So I did that sometimes if I was closer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you would see to it that first add was administered, would you, yourself, administer the first aid to soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There was a team of nurses and they would be on duty assigned, five nurses, and it was their duty to see to all that. The doctor would tell them what to administer, whether an intravenous drip or painkillers, or whatever, and if there was a fracture or an injury, then they would have to stop the bleeding and bandage the wound, put them into the vehicle, pack them up and send them off, depending on the need. Sometimes it would just be a nurse, nurses, sometimes a doctor, depending on how serious the case was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you approximate for us how many times were you called to do this duty, to go to the front line and transport injured soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you an exact number. In a year, perhaps 20, 50 times in a year, depending who was closest, and then some vehicles would break down so one vehicle would start off and break down. They were all old. And then another car would have to come and take over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, while Mr. Vasiljevic was getting his leg X-rayed, did you go out on other calls or did you remain at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZIVORAD SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended. I think that day, I did go off somewhere because we received information that somebody who was wounded was to arrive. So I waited at least two hours, more than an hour, perhaps two hours, and while he was having his X-ray done -- we have an old X-ray machine and you have to do it all by hand. You have to have a solution which has to be heated up, everything has to be dried by hand. It was an old X-ray machine. You have to hang the x-rays up with clothes pegs, with pegs, and then it took time for the X-ray, the negative to dry. So it all lasted a long time, an hour, two hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
