utterances.text: Patients who needed to undergo surgery or to be treated in a hospital who required to be treated under secondary medical care were mostly sent to the hospital in Titovo Uzice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am particularly interested in the year 1992. Does this apply to that year as well?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it does apply to that year, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Telling us where and when you worked, you told us that sometime in May 1992, you returned to the health centre. So could you please explain how work was organised? Was it in any way different from what it used to be before when you were working in the same institution?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: The organisation of work was different. I left the health centre in peacetime and returned when the war was already underway. In peacetime, one knew exactly who did what, who gave orders to whom, and how you filled in certain forms and reports, how you obtained medicines and everything else. During the war, a certain degree of chaos set in in which services functioned, mostly thanks to the enthusiasm and initiative of individuals employed in that service, so that the conditions were very hard. Most of the treatment was given in the emergency service. The occupational medicine service functioned only for a short time after the war broke out, whereas the other services more or less withered away and all activities focused primarily on treating serious and less serious conditions according to a special timetable which I can describe, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this, please, Mr. Loncarevic. Does that mean that you and the other doctors and medical staff had to work longer hours and to have -- be on duty longer?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The situation differed, depending on the various staff members. The males, the men who were in the records of the Defence department as able-bodied, and there were three of us on that list, three of us colleagues, we were obliged to be at the health centre almost continuously. We were given leave only occasionally to go home so as to change, have a bath, and occasionally to spend the night. The others, and I am referring in the first place to doctors who were not military conscripts, that is, who were not fit for military service, had assignments and they would be on duty in the emergency service or wherever necessary, together with us who were there most of the time, so that most frequently, we would have two, three, sometimes more doctors present simultaneously, depending on the needs. The nurses also had their own timetable of work which, in those days, was probably compiled by the director. I'm not quite sure who was in charge of the organisation of work, but I think it must have been the general manager who drafted the timetables, and this also applied to the other staff members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, do we need this sort of detail? This doctor is being called to prove one thing, that the accused came to him on a particular day and time and he sent him on to Uzice. Now, we don't need to know how the whole hospital works in order to establish that. Please lead him to the part which is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe this was a slightly more detailed answer than I expected but I thought it necessary to explain the conditions under which this centre was operating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My only additional question was whether, in that area, there was a military hospital separate from this institution.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no military hospital in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Loncarevic. My next question is: Do you know Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic or did you know him in the period we are referring to, that is, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know Mitar Vasiljevic. Before that time and during that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when have you known him and how?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I knew him several years before the war. I remember that he used to work as a waiter in a small coffee bar called Mezalin, and I would see him occasionally in other Panos establishments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, Dr. Loncarevic, you told us that in 1992 you left Visegrad in peacetime and you returned in wartime. That period when you came back and when you were working in the health centre, did you have occasion to see Mitar Vasiljevic primarily in town or somewhere else in town or the surroundings?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing Mitar Vasiljevic in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of what you told us a moment ago about your obligations as part of your military duties, did you often go into the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I already said that I rarely went home, but I live in an area that is below the town, that is close to the second bridge, and you don't have to pass through the town if you use that bridge. Very rarely, virtually never, did I go on foot. I went by car, crossing that new bridge, so that I didn't pass through the town centre. That may be the reason, if I may have come across him, though I can't talk about that because I do not remember, so my answer is I didn't come across Mitar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So during that period of time, did you see him in the health centre in which you were employed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain what particular time period you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to the period from which you returned, that is in May 1992 onwards. Since you have already told us that you didn't see him in town, did you see him in any other area or situation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was present in the health centre when the injured Vasiljevic was brought there. I don't remember whether we had any conversations. Vasiljevic, as far as I can recollect the situation, he was on a stretcher. Now, whether we first had contact within the hospital, within the centre compound or in the actual doctor's office, I can't say. It was a long time ago, but I seem to remember the image. I have the image in my mind of the injured man and several men who were carrying Mitar Vasiljevic towards the X-ray, because on the basis of an external and superficial examination, I was able to reach the conclusion that this was an injury or, rather, a fracture of the lower leg, and that is why I gave instructions for an X-ray to be made. Among the many images that have probably been wiped out of my memory, one remains clear, and that is this movement towards the X-ray from the steps to the door of the X-ray room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Loncarevic, if I understood you correctly, you first examined Mr. Vasiljevic, and on the basis of your external examination, you established that it was a fracture was involved and you sent him to have his X-ray taken; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it -- I assume it was the leg. I don't know whether you mentioned -- whether you told us what kind of fracture it was, of what part of the body?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the leg was X-rayed. The X-rays were done from two positions. I don't know whether it was all on one negative or two. I also cannot assert with certainty whether it was one or two bones of the left lower leg were broken. Judging by external signs, which I gave a lot of thought to subsequently, it is more probable that both bones were broken, but it is not something that I can assert with certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please explain a little what you meant, two shot? Are they two subsequent shots or two shots taken from different positions, different angles?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: The rule is, and that is a hard and fast rule, that every injury, especially when a fracture is suspected, that two different directions -- from two different directions an X-ray should be made so as to get more information about the time and type of injury. So it is possible to do this on one negative, or you may use two negatives, but the rule is to do so once from one angle, usually from the front, and a second time from a different position, that is, from the side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Loncarevic, will you tell us when these X-rays were made, what kind of x-ray equipment did you have in your health centre?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: In the health centre, we had an old X-ray. I am unable to say when this apparatus was manufactured, but it was operational, but the procedure for X-raying was rather specific. That is not so much the actual X-raying as the developing of the film itself. To develop the film, we had a bowl, a copper bowl, that the heaters were sunk into to warm up the chemicals used to develop the film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, again, do we need this sort of detail? Is there something that you have to explain about the quality of the X-rays which were taken? The fact is we've been told X-rays were taken and they were sent with him to Uzice. Do we need this?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I understand from the testimony of this witness is that these films were developed by hand and that is why I inquired as to the method of developing the film. Maybe the witness is going into considerable detail but let me shorten his answer by asking:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the developing done by hand and how long would it take for such a film to be developed? How much time was needed from the moment the X-ray was taken until you obtained the picture? Those are my questions and I think that they are relevant for this case.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were hand-developed, and to do this, you need about 20 minutes, sometimes longer, sometimes less, but around 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the developing of these X-rays, do you know what happened then with Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic was carried back to the room for treatment, where he was given emergency treatment and prepared for transport which means that the injured leg was immobilised and everything else that was necessary was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned immobilisation and preparation for transport. For transport where, Mr. Loncarevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: For transport to the hospital in Titovo Uzice, the orthopaedics ward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For such transport, was it necessary for one of you in the health centre in Visegrad to prepare a referral document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was necessary. The referral letter needed to be drafted because the patient would not have been admitted to hospital without a referral letter. I cannot remember who wrote that referral. I gave instructions for this to be done and I knew that it was something that we had to do. Now, whether I wrote that referral or one of my colleagues did, I don't remember now even who it was among my colleagues that were present so I can't assert that now. In any event, a referral letter had to be written.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In such situations, Mr. Loncarevic, when you are sending a patient with referral to another institution, to the hospital in Uzice in this particular case, in addition to the referral letter, does the patient carry anything else with him as his documentation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: The rule is that a patient, in addition to the referral, should carry with him any other documents he has. In this case, it must have been the X-ray that was done. It is true that I didn't see it or see him carrying it, so I can't claim that, but I wish to say that that is the rule and it was never deviated from. Whether it was done in this case, I can't claim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Loncarevic, talking about the X-ray, how is an X-ray picture marked, if marked at all, before it is given to the patient?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly there are some markings made on the X-ray. The first and last name of the patient must be written on the X-ray, the date when it was done, and which side was filmed, was it the left or the right side, which is marked with a capital "L" or a capital "D" in the Latin script.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those days, how was -- were these markings made, with a typewriter or by hand?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, we didn't have any equipment to be able to make such inscriptions automatically so I think we used a water resistant marker, a simple ordinary marker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who would make those markings? Would it be the doctor or the technician operating the X-ray machine?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: These markings would be made by the X-ray technicians and he carries out the actual filming and he makes the markings on the film too?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loncarevic, can you tell us, to the best of your recollection, what time of day it was when Mr. Vasiljevic was carried into the health centre on a stretcher?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I cannot claim with precision because, after all, it was a very long time ago so I can't remember the exact time. What I am able to say is that it was daytime, that I am sure of. That is something I can claim. As far as I am able to recollect, I think I had finished lunch and it wasn't close to nightfall. It was a cloudy day. I think that it was also -- there was a fine rain falling. If I were to have to give some closer indication of the time, I would prefer to say that it was sometime around 4.00 p.m. or between 4.00 and 6.00 p.m., sometime there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned your lunch; as an orientation, around what time would you normally have lunch in those days?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Then and now, my custom was to have lunch around 3.00 p.m., sometimes a little earlier, sometimes a little later, of course in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those days, was it required that a vehicle belonging to the health centre transport, in this case, Mitar Vasiljevic, to Uzice?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that a vehicle was required which allowed the patient to be in lying down position, it had to be our vehicle and there was no reason to use any other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think that might be an appropriate time, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I make a brief request before we finish business for the day? I make this request just in an abundance of caution, not casting aspersions in any direction, but could I ask the Court to perhaps direct the Victims and Witness Service to advise Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Savic that if he has any concerns for his safety now or upon his return, that he should call them and discuss those concerns with Victims and Witness Services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask the Court Deputy to pass on your message, but it may be better if somebody from the Prosecution explained it to them. I wouldn't expect us to buy into any conclusions, but there are obviously great possibilities, and I would agree with you that the warning would be very appropriate, but I think it might be a good idea if you added the weight to the detail involved so they know what it is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. 9.30 in the morning
